title: All gone now
hook: a king's golden palaces and elephants, every one of them gone
carry: it was grand once, and it's gone

segments.voice: Yesterday: relics shared among eight peoples, and the Buddha's last words. Your line: strive on. Today closes a week, with a story the Buddha told about the little town where he died.

Kusinara was not much of a place. In the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, Ananda pleads with the Buddha: please don't pass away in this little wattle-and-daub town, out in the jungle. There are great cities: Rajagaha, Savatthi, Varanasi. Go there. And the Buddha says: don't call it that, Ananda. Long ago, this was a royal city, and he begins to describe it. The seventeenth Long Discourse tells the whole story.
screen: `A LITTLE WATTLE-AND-DAUB TOWN.` → `DON'T CALL IT THAT.` → `ONCE A ROYAL CITY.`

segments.voice: The city was called Kusavati, and its king was Mahasudassana, the great and beautiful. The sutta lingers on every detail. Seven walls, of gold, silver, beryl, crystal and more. Rows of palm trees made of jewels, and when the wind moved their leaves, the sound was sweet and lovely, like a well-played orchestra, so that the people who heard it danced. Eighty-four thousand cities, eighty-four thousand palaces, eighty-four thousand elephants with golden trappings, chariots, horses, gems, and a whole court around him. The king was good, too. He gave freely, and in a palace built for him he sat alone and practiced, letting a mind of loving-kindness, compassion, gladness and calm fill every direction: the same practice as the trumpeter on day five hundred forty-two. And then the turn. Out of all those palaces, the king lived in only one. Out of all those elephants, he rode only one. And at the end, the Buddha tells Ananda: I was that king. And see, Ananda, all those things are past, ceased, changed. That is how impermanent conditioned things are. It's a strange kind of comfort. The Buddha is lying in a poor village, and he doesn't argue that it's secretly grand. He says it was grand once, and it's gone, as everything grand goes. Look back at this week: no closed fist, the four great references, the four places, Ananda in the doorway, the teaching as teacher, the relics shared, and now a golden city gone back to mud and thatch.
screen: `KUSAVATI, THE CITY OF JEWELS.` · `PALM TREES THAT MADE MUSIC.` · `HE LIVED IN ONLY ONE PALACE.` · `I WAS THAT KING.` · then, large: `ALL GONE NOW.`

segments.voice: Look at one fine thing near you, a cup you like, a plant, the light on a wall, kindly and fully, as if it's the best palace in the city. Then close your eyes and let yourself know it won't last forever, not with sadness, just with honesty. Keep the kindness and the honesty together, and breathe.
Anicca. The Mahasudassana Sutta's ending: a king's jeweled city, palaces and elephants, all past, ceased and changed. Today's word.
Your line: it was grand once, and it's gone. A fine thing is no less fine for passing. That closes the week.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the Mahasudassana story to teach impermanence, and at funerals in Theravada countries monks chant the verse beginning 'anicca vata sankhara', impermanent indeed are conditioned things.

fork.setup: Ananda begs you not to die in a humble jungle village. what do you, the Buddha, say?
options: agree, and set off for a great city.
tell him it was once a royal city, and that all its splendor has passed.
say that places don't matter at all.
fork.reveal: he tells the story of Kusavati and ends: all those things are past, ceased, changed.

original.note: Pali anicca: impermanent. the lesson the Buddha draws from the vanished city.

trapdoor: what you thought: Kusinara was just a poor village.
what it means: in the Buddha's telling it was once Kusavati, a jeweled royal city, now all gone.
what a scholar hears: DN 17 expands a short passage in DN 16 into a full narrative and closes on impermanence; it is also a jataka-like story, with the Buddha naming himself as the king.

chat.says: Why did the dying Buddha tell Ananda about a jeweled city at Kusinara?
options: To show that everything grand passes: the city was splendid once, and it's gone.
To prove Kusinara was secretly still grand, so a fine place to die.
To say only great cities are worthy places for a Buddha to die.
chat.meaning: He says the humble village was once Kusavati, a jeweled royal city, and he was its king: all of it past, ceased, changed.

Kusavati.meaning: the jeweled royal city that Kusinara once was
